analysis.one_liner: Creates mandatory federal inspection and safety standards for all seafood sold in the United States.
analysis.headline: A House committee approved mandatory inspection of all U.S. and imported seafood in October 1990, but the bill died without a floor vote in either chamber.
analysis.plain_summary: Seafood was the only major food without mandatory federal inspection. This bill would have created a comprehensive safety program covering fishing vessels, processing plants, and imports: federal safety standards, limits on contaminants, authority to close contaminated shellfish harvesting waters, recall power, CDC tracking of seafood-borne illness, and protections for workers who refuse unsafe work. The House committee approved an expanded version in October 1990, but the bill never came up for a vote before the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Seafood consumers, who would get inspected products, contaminant limits set at levels not injurious to health, labeled and certified imports, and government recalls of adulterated products. Shellfish eaters specifically gain a program to test growing waters and close contaminated harvesting areas. Reputable seafood firms gain a level playing field against sellers of poor-quality products, and plant workers gain whistleblower protections.

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a comprehensive inspection program for fish products covering harvesting, processing, storing, transportation, and marketing, so consumers get products checked for adulteration from boat to shelf.

Creates a National Shellfish Safety Program with standards for growing waters, water quality, and contaminants, and lets regulators close harvesting areas that fail or threaten public health — targeting the shellfish that cause many seafood illness outbreaks.

Tightens the border: all fish products from nations without a certified equivalent safety program must be inspected on entry, with random sampling even from certified nations, and importers must be certified annually.
Requires FDA to set health-based tolerances for poisons, chemicals, bacteria, viruses, and parasites in fish, based on scientific risk analysis.
Gives the government authority to recall adulterated or misbranded seafood and bans false or misleading labeling and packaging.
Directs the CDC to build a surveillance system estimating how often Americans get sick from seafood, replacing guesswork with data.
Protects seafood workers: an employee who refuses to perform work that violates the law cannot be discriminated against, and can take a complaint to the Labor Secretary.
Federal funds cover the cost of inspections (except overtime and holidays), and states with approved programs can receive up to 50 percent of the cost of running an equivalent state program.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the inspection system — $90 million per year was authorized for fiscal 1990 through 1993, and the bill requires the federal government to bear inspection costs except overtime and holiday work. Seafood processors, harvesters, and importers bear the compliance costs: certification, sanitary standards, record-keeping, labeling, possible facility upgrades, and reduced harvests in areas closed for contamination. Some of those costs could be passed to consumers in the form of higher seafood prices.

drawbacks.text: The public cost is real: $90 million per year authorized for four fiscal years, with the government required to pay for inspections, plus up to 50 percent matching grants to states for their own programs.

The program's protections were contingent on funding: the Secretary could exempt handling or processing from inspection requirements until July 1, 1995 if appropriated funds made inspection impractical, meaning the program could be hollowed out if Congress underfunded it.

Compliance costs fall hardest on smaller processors and importers, who must certify, register, meet sanitary standards, and keep origin and processing records; some of these costs would likely be passed on to shoppers as higher seafood prices.

Common carriers and distributors got a liability carve-out: they face no penalties for transporting adulterated seafood unless they knew or should have known about it, weakening accountability in the distribution chain.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — closing the last major gap in federal food inspection, at a time when contaminated shellfish and adulterated imports were documented problems — outweighs a modest public cost of roughly $90 million a year, with inspections largely government-paid rather than adding a per-plant fee burden. The honest caveats: the enforcement carve-out for common carriers dilutes accountability in distribution, and the funding-contingent exemption through 1995 meant the promised inspection regime could have been postponed if Congress stinted on appropriations.

outcome.mechanism: The House committee approved an expanded version in mid-October 1990 and the bill was placed on the House calendar, but House leaders never brought it to the floor before the two-year Congress ended in January 1991, so the Senate never considered it.

narrative.text: Representative Gerry Studds, the Democratic chairman of the House Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committee, introduced the bill on May 25, 1989 together with the senior Republican on that committee, Don Young of Alaska; it authorized $90 million a year for fiscal 1990 through 1993.
The subcommittee held hearings in June and November 1989, then amended and forwarded the bill to the full committee in July 1990.

The full committee amended it substantially — splitting it into a shellfish safety title and a comprehensive fish inspection title with import controls, recalls, CDC illness tracking, and whistleblower protections — and reported it to the House on October 15, 1990.

The bill was referred sequentially to the Energy and Commerce Committee for one day, discharged, and placed on the Union Calendar on October 16, 1990 — leaving roughly two and a half months before the 101st Congress expired.
No floor vote ever occurred, in either chamber, before the Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and the bill died with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Seafood processors and importers came out ahead: they avoided mandatory federal inspection, certification, and sanitary-standard compliance costs for the time being, and states with existing programs kept the voluntary status quo. Consumers continued to buy the only major food category with no mandatory federal inspection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Seafood processors and importers avoided inspection

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes were ever taken; sponsorship was bipartisan — the Democratic committee chairman introduced the bill with the senior Republican on his committee, and two of 175 House Republicans cosponsored.

industries.note: The bill imposes mandatory inspection, certification, sanitary standards, record-keeping, and labeling costs on processors and importers, with all shipments from uncertified nations inspected at the border. But it also gives compliant firms a federal seal and uniform national standards that build consumer confidence and squeeze out sellers of adulterated or mislabeled product, a trade-off the bill's own findings acknowledge.

The bill lets regulators close contaminated harvesting areas and sets handling and storage standards for fishing vessels, restricting harvesters' operations. In exchange, harvesters get federal aid flowing to state monitoring programs and a public-health seal of approval for their catch.

industries.industry: Seafood wholesalers, distributors, and common carriers
industries.note: The bill exempts common carriers from penalties for transporting adulterated or misbranded seafood unless they knew or had facts that would cause a reasonable person to know. This liability shield puts less accountability in the middle of the distribution chain, where consumers cannot see it.
